title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: SASB. Full Name: Sustainability Accounting Standards Board. Focus: Industry-specific ESG performance. Scope: Global, with focus on U.S. companies. Reporting Requirement: Voluntary, but often integrated in financial disclosures. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with TCFD, GRI. Industry-Specific Guidance: Yes, 77 industry-specific standards. Key Features: Focuses on financially material sustainability issues relevant to investors

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: SBTi. Full Name: Science-Based Targets initiative. Focus: Climate goals, GHG emissions reductions. Scope: Global. Reporting Requirement: Voluntary; companies commit to setting science-based emissions reduction targets. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with CDP, TCFD, Paris Agreement. Industry-Specific Guidance: No, but applicable to various sectors. Key Features: Focuses on aligning corporate emissions reduction targets with scientific goals (e.g., limiting global warming to 1.5°C)

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: CSRD. Full Name: Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive. Focus: Comprehensive sustainability reporting. Scope: EU companies and non-EU companies operating in the EU. Reporting Requirement: Mandatory for large EU companies, phased approach starting in 2024. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with European Green Deal, GRI. Industry-Specific Guidance: No, but includes sector-specific indicators. Key Features: Expands on NFRD, integrates double materiality (financial + sustainability impact)

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: TCFD. Full Name: Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Focus: Climate-related financial risk. Scope: Global. Reporting Requirement: Voluntary, but increasingly adopted in mandatory disclosure regimes. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with SASB, CDP, GRI. Industry-Specific Guidance: No, general recommendations for all sectors. Key Features: Emphasizes financial impact of climate risks, scenario analysis

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: GRI. Full Name: Global Reporting Initiative. Focus: Broad sustainability impacts (ESG). Scope: Global. Reporting Requirement: Voluntary but widely adopted. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with SASB, UN SDGs. Industry-Specific Guidance: Yes, sector standards available. Key Features: Focuses on the wider impact of sustainability on stakeholders, beyond financial materiality

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: CDP. Full Name: Carbon Disclosure Project. Focus: Environmental impact, particularly carbon emissions. Scope: Global. Reporting Requirement: Voluntary, but used by investors and governments. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with SBTi, TCFD, GRI. Industry-Specific Guidance: No, broad coverage across sectors. Key Features: Focuses on environmental disclosures, especially climate and water security

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: ISSB. Full Name: International Sustainability Standards Board. Focus: Comprehensive global sustainability standards. Scope: Global. Reporting Requirement: Mandatory (in some jurisdictions), voluntary elsewhere. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with TCFD, SASB, IFRS. Industry-Specific Guidance: No, but builds on SASB’s industry-specific approach. Key Features: Aims to create globally consistent, comparable sustainability standards, integrates financial materiality

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Framework/Standard: NFRD. Full Name: Non-Financial Reporting Directive. Focus: Sustainability-related disclosures for large companies. Scope: EU. Reporting Requirement: Mandatory for large EU public-interest entities. Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with GRI, TCFD. Industry-Specific Guidance: No, broad applicability across sectors. Key Features: Predecessor to CSRD, focuses on non-financial reporting requirements in the EU

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: Key Takeaways: SASB and SBTi focus on industry-specific guidance and emissions targets, respectively, with emphasis on financial materiality (SASB) and climate science (SBTi). CSRD introduces mandatory, comprehensive sustainability reporting in the EU, with an emphasis on double materiality. GRI takes a broader, stakeholder-focused approach, while TCFD and CDP emphasize climate-related financial risk and environmental disclosures. ISSB aims to unify global sustainability standards for consistent and comparable reporting.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: ESG standards set specific and detailed technical requirements on how sustainability data should be measured, reported, and verified. Standards define the exact methodology and metrics companies must use—creating consistency that enables meaningful comparison of ESG performance across time, industry, and size. Most standards are voluntary and provide supplementary guidance on reporting language, format, and instructions for applying the standard based on unique business characteristics. Examples of global reporting standards include the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB).

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: While there is no single, universally mandated ESG standard, a few of the most widely recognized and adopted ones are below.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: The International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) Sustainability Disclosure Standards, developed by the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB), are designed to help investors and capital markets assess and disclose sustainability-related risks and opportunities. Its first two standards—IFRS S1 (general sustainability-related financial disclosures) and IFRS S2 (climate-related disclosures)—were published in 2023 and are now seeing rapid regulatory uptake, with over 36 jurisdictions committed to aligning with them.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: The Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), part of the IFRS Foundation, developed industry-specific disclosure guidance on sustainability-related risks and opportunities covering 77 industries. The standards are designed to identify the most relevant environmental, social, and governance issues that may impact the financial performance and overall enterprise value of an organization. Its open standard-setting approach allows more flexibility to determine what ESG topics are financially material to a business.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: The Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME) offers a streamlined, accessible alternative to the ESRS, helping small and medium-sized enterprises report on sustainability performance in a way that is proportionate to their business needs. The VSME helps SMEs respond to ESG demands from investors and corporate partners in their value chain, improving risk management and access to capital. With Basic and Comprehensive modules, companies have the flexibility to report based on what’s relevant and their reporting readiness. Aligned with the EU Omnibus I proposal and its “value chain cap” on sustainability data requests, the VSME enables SMEs to demonstrate resilience, manage climate risks, and prepare for evolving regulations.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards are known as the most widely used standards for sustainability reporting, with over 70% of leading companies globally adopting it as a primary framework for disclosing ESG impact. The GRI standards are built on the principle of impact materiality, requiring organizations to report on how their activities affect the economy, environment, and society.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: ESG frameworks provide a broad, contextual approach to ESG reporting. Rather than prescribing specific metrics, frameworks define the themes, objectives, and scope of sustainability reporting, guiding companies on what topics to address, the data to collect, and how reporting should be presented. ESG frameworks are largely voluntary, and widely accepted frameworks include the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosure (TCFD), the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP), or the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: There are many frameworks that support ESG reporting, and here are some of the most widely accepted frameworks.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: The Task Force for Climate-Related Disclosures (TCFD), established by the Financial Stability Board in 2015, was developed to guide disclosure recommendations for climate-related financial information. It enables companies to be more transparent on their climate-related risk exposures to investors, lenders and insurance underwriters. The TCFD is comprised of 11 recommendations structured around four pillars: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets. While the TCFD disbanded in October 2023, the IFRS foundation officially incorporated the full TCFD recommendations in its publication of IFRS S1 and S2 standards. TCFD as a framework continues to be the blueprint for many emerging frameworks and regulations, including California’s SB 261. TCFD-aligned disclosures are now mandatory in many jurisdictions globally, including the UK, Japan, and New Zealand.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: CDP, formerly known as the Carbon Disclosure Project, is an international nonprofit organization that provides the world’s leading environmental impact disclosure system. It enables investors, companies, cities, states, and regions to assess their greenhouse gas emissions and climate risks, driving emissions reductions and strengthening climate resilience. CDP collects and standardizes environmental data through a voluntary basis to better inform corporate and city progress towards climate change, forests, and water security goals through an independent scoring methodology.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: Invest Europe is the association representing Europe’s private equity, venture capital, and infrastructure sectors, as well as their investors. Its voluntary, principles-based ESG framework is developed specifically for European firms in the private equity and venture capital space and provides guidance on how investors can integrate ESG considerations into the entire investment lifecycle, from evaluation to exit. Invest Europe manages an ESG reporting template for reporting at the portfolio company, GP, and fund levels.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: The ESG Data Convergence Initiative (EDCI) is a global private markets initiative committed to streamlining the industry’s historically fragmented approach to collecting and reporting sustainability data. The EDCI’s mission is to drive convergence around sustainability metrics to enable meaningful, comparable reporting. Its core metric categories are reviewed annually for relevancy, which currently include greenhouse gas emissions, diversity, and employee engagement. UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a set of 17 interconnected global goals designed to address the world’s most pressing social, environmental, and economic challenges by 2030—spanning areas such as climate action, clean energy, gender equality, and responsible consumption. For companies and investors, the SDGs serve as a high-level framework for aligning business strategy and capital allocation with broader societal outcomes.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
section: Why ESG Frameworks and Standards Are Important
text: With ESG constantly evolving, frameworks and standards help reduce ambiguity and complexity in reporting. They offer a shared language for sustainability disclosures that enables organizations to report reliable, decision-useful data. This consistency also ensures that the reported information remains comparable across peers, industries, and over time for true, meaningful ESG progress.

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
section: The Differences Between ESG Standards and Frameworks
text: The terms “frameworks” and “standards” are often used interchangeably in ESG reporting, but they each serve a distinct purpose. ESG frameworks are broad and provide a contextual “frame” on how to disclose material topics in reporting. They provide a high-level structure and guiding principles on how data should be presented. Take the TCFD, for example, which provides a framework to report climate-related financial disclosures but leaves the specific data points to the reporting company. ESG standards, on the other hand, are specific and prescriptive. They define the exact metrics and methodologies that should be disclosed. Standards are valuable for investors who need to compare ESG performance across a portfolio or industry benchmark, as they allow for consistent year-on-year tracking. In practice, many organizations use frameworks and standards together. Frameworks are applied to shape the structure of the report, while standards ensure that the reported data is rigorous, consistent, and comparable.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: These three are voluntary on their own, but nearly every mandatory regime below is built on them. They become enforceable only when a jurisdiction writes them into law.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 1. ISSB Standards (IFRS S1 and S2). The investor-focused global baseline from the IFRS Foundation. Components: S1 covers general sustainability-related financial information; S2 covers climate. Both use the four TCFD pillars (governance, strategy, risk management, metrics and targets), require Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions and climate scenario analysis, and apply a financial materiality lens. In scope: Any company may apply them. As of April 2026, 28 jurisdictions had adopted them on a voluntary or mandatory basis and 12 more planned to (S&P Global). Australia, Japan, the UK and Brazil have issued ISSB-based standards. Enforcement: None from the ISSB itself; enforced by the regulators that adopt it.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 2. GRI Standards. The most widely used impact-focused framework, aimed at all stakeholders rather than only investors. Components: Universal Standards (GRI 1 to 3), 30+ topic standards and sector standards, built on impact materiality. New GRI 102 (Climate Change) and GRI 103 (Energy) apply to reports published from 1 January 2027, adding transition plan, just transition and carbon credit disclosures (GRI). In scope: Voluntary for any organization of any size or sector. Enforcement: None. Claiming "in accordance with GRI" requires a content index and notification to GRI; ESRS is designed to be interoperable with it.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 3. GHG Protocol. The accounting rulebook for emissions that every regime in this briefing relies on. Components: Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance (location- and market-based methods) and Scope 3 Standard (15 value chain categories). A revision under consultation would require hourly and regional matching of renewable energy certificates for market-based Scope 2 claims, with a final standard expected in 2027 and implementation likely from 2028 (Greenplaces). In scope: Voluntary; referenced directly by California SB 253, ISSB, AASB S2 and ESRS. Enforcement: None of its own; errors are penalized through the laws that reference it.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: The EU remains the most demanding jurisdiction, but the Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force since 18 March 2026, cut the number of companies in scope by roughly 80% (Norton Rose Fulbright). Member States must transpose it into national law.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
section: 4. Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and ESRS
text: 4. Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and ESRS. The EU's mandatory sustainability reporting law and its technical standards. Components: Double materiality (impacts on people and planet, plus financial risk); 2 cross-cutting and 10 topical ESRS; mandatory limited assurance; digital tagging, now postponed. Revised ESRS adopted on 3 July 2026 cut mandatory datapoints by over 60% and total datapoints by over 70% (European Commission). In scope: EU companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450m net turnover. Non-EU groups are in scope with over EUR 450m EU turnover and an EU subsidiary or branch above EUR 200m (Latham & Watkins). Suppliers under 1,000 employees can decline data requests beyond a voluntary SME standard. Enforcement: Penalties set by each Member State; statutory auditors or accredited assurers sign off; national market regulators supervise listed issuers.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 5. EU Taxonomy Regulation. A classification system defining which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable. Components: Six environmental objectives; an activity is "aligned" if it substantially contributes to one, does no significant harm to the others and meets minimum social safeguards. Companies report the share of turnover, CapEx and OpEx that is eligible and aligned. Since January 2026, activities below 10% of a KPI can be excluded from detailed assessment and templates are about 64% shorter (BCLP). In scope: Companies subject to CSRD (Article 8), plus financial market participants through SFDR. Enforcement: Through the CSRD and SFDR supervisory regimes above.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 6. Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR). Disclosure rules for asset managers, insurers, pension funds and advisers. Components: Entity-level principal adverse impact statements and product labels under Article 8 ("promotes" ESG) and Article 9 (sustainable objective). SFDR 2.0 would replace these with three categories (Sustainable, Transition and ESG Basics), each requiring 70% of assets to meet the category's criteria. The Council agreed its position in June 2026 and Parliament's committee in September 2026; trilogues are expected to start in October (RankiaPro). In scope: Financial market participants and advisers marketing products in the EU, including non-EU managers. Enforcement: National financial regulators, with ESMA coordinating; greenwashing in fund names and marketing is an active enforcement priority.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 7. Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD). A conduct obligation, not only a disclosure one. Components: Identify, prevent and remediate adverse human rights and environmental impacts in the company's own operations and chain of activities, with a risk-based focus. In scope: EU companies with more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn net worldwide turnover, and non-EU companies with EUR 1.5bn EU turnover. Compliance is required from 26 July 2029 (Morrison Foerster). Enforcement: National supervisory authorities with administrative fines; the Omnibus narrowed the liability and penalty provisions (Accountancy Europe).

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: There is no federal mandate; California is the binding regime. The SEC's 2024 climate rule never took effect: it was stayed in 2024, the SEC stopped defending it in March 2025 and proposed rescinding it on 29 May 2026. Until a final rescission, the rule stays stayed and the SEC's 2010 interpretive guidance on material climate risk still applies (Jones Day).

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 8. California SB 253 and SB 261. Two companion laws administered by the California Air Resources Board (CARB). Components: SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) requires annual Scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting from 2026 and Scope 3 from 2027, measured under the GHG Protocol, with third-party assurance phasing from limited to reasonable. SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act) requires a biennial public report on climate-related financial risk and mitigation, which may follow TCFD or ISSB. In scope: US-organized entities doing business in California with total annual revenue above $1bn (SB 253) or above $500m (SB 261), public or private, measured globally (Persefoni). Status: CARB moved the first SB 253 deadline from 10 August to 10 November 2026 and will not require assurance on that first report (Baker Tilly). A Ninth Circuit injunction has paused SB 261 enforcement since November 2025; a ruling on the First Amendment challenge was still pending as of August 2026. Enforcement: CARB administrative penalties of up to $500,000 per reporting year under SB 253 and up to $50,000 under SB 261. Scope 3 misstatements are protected by a safe harbor if made in good faith, and penalties for Scope 3 are limited to non-filing until 2030.

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: 9. Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards (AASB S2). Mandatory climate reporting under Chapter 2M of the Corporations Act 2001, based on IFRS S2. Components: A sustainability report lodged with the annual report, covering governance, strategy, risk management and metrics; Scope 1 and 2 emissions from year one and Scope 3 from year two; scenario analysis at 1.5°C and at 2.5°C or higher; a directors' declaration; assurance phasing from limited to reasonable. AASB S1 (general sustainability) is voluntary. In scope: Entities that lodge annual reports and meet two of three size tests, phased by group. Group 1 began with years starting 1 January 2025 (revenue A$500m, assets A$1bn, 500 employees). Group 2 began with years starting 1 July 2026 (A$200m, A$500m, 250 employees). Group 3 follows from 1 July 2027 (A$50m, A$25m, 100 employees) (Carbon Impact). Large emitters under the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Act and large asset owners are also caught. Enforcement: ASIC, under the same civil penalty and director liability provisions as financial reports. A three-year "modified liability" period limits claims over Scope 3, scenario analysis and transition plans to ASIC-only actions (Naturaliste).

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
section: 10. Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) and BRSR Core
text: 10. Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) and BRSR Core. India's mandatory ESG report, set by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). Components: Full BRSR covers the nine principles of India's National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct, from environment to employee welfare to consumer fairness. BRSR Core is a subset of nine attributes (including GHG emissions, water, energy, waste, gender diversity and workforce safety) that must be independently assessed or assured. In scope: The top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalization file the full BRSR. BRSR Core assessment or assurance extends to all 1,000 from FY 2026-27. Value chain disclosures for the top 250 are voluntary from FY 2025-26 after SEBI's March 2025 deferral (Sustainability 101). Enforcement: A listing obligation under SEBI's LODR Regulation 34(2)(f), filed with the annual report; SEBI and the stock exchanges can impose fines and other actions for non-compliance or misstatement.

title: Double Materiality
text: Double materiality is an emphasis in sustainability reporting, particularly within the CSRD, that integrates both financial materiality (impacts on financial performance) and impact materiality (impacts on people and planet). This approach is a key feature of the CSRD and is integrated into standards like the ISSB.

title: Double Materiality
text: - CSRD integrates double materiality, which includes impacts on people and planet plus financial risk [2, 3]. - The CSRD focuses on comprehensive sustainability reporting and aligns with the European Green Deal and GRI. (Comparison table, CSRD row) - In scope for CSRD, EU companies must have more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450m net turnover, or non-EU groups with over EUR 450m EU turnover and an EU subsidiary or branch above EUR 200m. (Briefing p.2) - The revised ESRS adopted on 3 July 2026 will cut mandatory datapoints by over 60% and total datapoints by over 70%. (Briefing p.2) - ISSB aims to create globally consistent, comparable sustainability standards and integrates financial materiality. (Comparison table, ISSB row) - GRI standards are built on the principle of impact materiality, requiring organizations to report on how their activities affect the economy, environment, and society. (Novata p.3)

title: Scope 1 2 and 3 Emissions
text: This note outlines the requirements for Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions reporting under various ESG frameworks and regulations. It highlights that different regimes mandate reporting based on their specific laws and standards, such as California's SB 253 and the ISSB standards.

title: Scope 1 2 and 3 Emissions
text: - California SB 253 requires annual Scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting starting from 2026, with Scope 3 reporting required from 2027. (Briefing pp.3-4) - The GHG Protocol is the accounting rulebook for emissions that every regime in this briefing relies on, including the Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance, and Scope 3 Standard. (Briefing pp.1-2) - ISSB Standards (IFRS S1 and S2) require companies to report Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions and climate scenario analysis. (Briefing p.1) - Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards (AASB S2) mandate Scope 1 and 2 emissions from year one and Scope 3 emissions from year two. (Briefing p.4) - SBTi focuses on setting science-based emissions reduction targets globally, which is a voluntary reporting requirement. (Comparison table, SBTi row) - CDP enables investors, companies, cities, states, and regions to assess greenhouse gas emissions and climate risks through a voluntary basis. (Novata p.4) - BRSR Core requires independent assessment or assurance for attributes including GHG emissions for the top 1,000 listed companies from FY 2026-27. (Briefing pp.4-5)

title: Standards vs Frameworks
text: ESG frameworks and standards serve distinct purposes in reporting; frameworks provide a broad structure and guiding principles, while standards define specific, prescriptive metrics and methodologies. They are often used together to ensure reports are both structured and rigorous.

title: Standards vs Frameworks
text: - ESG frameworks are broad and provide a contextual “frame” on how to disclose material topics in reporting, offering a high-level structure and guiding principles on data presentation. (Novata p.5) - ESG standards are specific and prescriptive, defining the exact metrics and methodologies that must be disclosed. (Novata p.5) - Frameworks define the themes, objectives, and scope of sustainability reporting, guiding companies on what topics to address, the data to collect, and how reporting should be presented, and are largely voluntary. (Novata p.3) - Standards set specific and detailed technical requirements on how sustainability data should be measured, reported, and verified, defining the exact methodology and metrics companies must use. (Novata pp.1-2) - Frameworks are applied to shape the structure of the report, while standards ensure that the reported data is rigorous, consistent, and comparable. (Novata p.5) - Frameworks are largely voluntary, with widely accepted examples including the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosure (TCFD), the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP), or the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). (Novata p.3) - Standards provide supplementary guidance on reporting language, format, and instructions for applying the standard based on unique business characteristics. (Novata pp.1-2)

title: CSDDD
text: The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) imposes a conduct obligation on companies to identify, prevent, and remediate adverse human rights and environmental impacts in their operations and supply chains. This directive applies to large EU and non-EU companies, requiring compliance starting from July 26, 2029.

title: CSDDD
text: - CSDDD is a conduct obligation, not just a disclosure one. (Briefing p.3) - Components of CSDDD include identifying, preventing, and remediating adverse human rights and environmental impacts in the company's own operations and chain of activities, with a risk-based focus. (Briefing p.3) - In scope are EU companies with more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn net worldwide turnover, and non-EU companies with EUR 1.5bn EU turnover. (Briefing p.3) - Compliance is required from 26 July 2029. (Briefing p.3) - Enforcement involves national supervisory authorities with administrative fines; the Omnibus narrowed the liability and penalty provisions. (Briefing p.3)

title: CSRD and ESRS
text: The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) is the EU's mandatory sustainability reporting law, which includes technical standards known as ESRS. This framework requires comprehensive reporting, focusing on double materiality, and applies to large EU companies and certain non-EU groups.

title: CSRD and ESRS
text: - CSRD components include double materiality (impacts on people and planet, plus financial risk), 2 cross-cutting and 10 topical ESRS, mandatory limited assurance, and digital tagging (now postponed). (Briefing p.2) - The revised ESRS adopted on 3 July 2026 cut mandatory datapoints by over 60% and total datapoints by over 70% (European Commission). (Briefing p.2) - In scope for CSRD are EU companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450m net turnover. (Briefing p.2) - Non-EU groups are in scope with over EUR 450m EU turnover and an EU subsidiary or branch above EUR 200m (Latham & Watkins). (Briefing p.2) - The CSRD is mandatory for large EU companies, with a phased approach starting in 2024. (Comparison table, CSRD row) - The CSRD aligns with the European Green Deal and GRI, and expands on NFRD by integrating double materiality (financial + sustainability impact). (Comparison table, CSRD row) - Enforcement involves penalties set by each Member State, sign-off by statutory auditors or accredited assurers, and supervision by national market regulators for listed issuers. (Briefing p.2)

title: EU Taxonomy
text: The EU Taxonomy is a classification system that defines which economic activities are considered environmentally sustainable. It is important because companies report the share of turnover, CapEx, and OpEx that is eligible and aligned with these objectives.

title: EU Taxonomy
text: - It is a classification system defining which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable. (Briefing p.2) - Components include six environmental objectives; an activity is "aligned" if it substantially contributes to one, does no significant harm to the others and meets minimum social safeguards. (Briefing p.2) - Companies report the share of turnover, CapEx and OpEx that is eligible and aligned. (Briefing p.2) - Since January 2026, activities below 10% of a KPI can be excluded from detailed assessment and templates are about 64% shorter (BCLP). (Briefing p.2) - In scope are companies subject to CSRD (Article 8), plus financial market participants through SFDR. (Briefing p.2) - Enforcement is through the CSRD and SFDR supervisory regimes. (Briefing p.2)

title: NFRD
text: The Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) is a directive focused on sustainability-related disclosures for large companies within the EU. It is significant as it serves as the predecessor to the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD).

title: NFRD
text: - Full Name: Non-Financial Reporting Directive. (Comparison table, NFRD row) - Focus: Sustainability-related disclosures for large companies. (Comparison table, NFRD row) - Scope: EU. (Comparison table, NFRD row) - Reporting Requirement: Mandatory for large EU public-interest entities. (Comparison table, NFRD row) - Alignment with Other Standards: Aligned with GRI, TCFD. (Comparison table, NFRD row) - Key Features: Predecessor to CSRD, focuses on non-financial reporting requirements in the EU. (Comparison table, NFRD row)

title: Omnibus I Directive
text: The Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force since 18 March 2026, is a 2026 EU simplification package that reduced the number of companies in scope by roughly 80%. It also relates to changes concerning the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) and introduces alternatives like the Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME). (Briefing p.2, Novata pp.2-3)

title: Omnibus I Directive
text: - The Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470 is in force since 18 March 2026. (Briefing p.2) - The Directive cut the number of companies in scope by roughly 80%. (Briefing p.2) - Member States must transpose the Omnibus I Directive into national law. (Briefing p.2) - The Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME) offers a streamlined, accessible alternative to the ESRS. (Novata pp.2-3) - The VSME helps SMEs report on sustainability performance in a way that is proportionate to their business needs. (Novata pp.2-3) - The VSME enables SMEs to demonstrate resilience, manage climate risks, and prepare for evolving regulations, aligned with the EU Omnibus I proposal and its “value chain cap” on sustainability data requests. (Novata pp.2-3) - The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) requires compliance from 26 July 2029. (Briefing p.3) - In scope for CSDDD, EU companies must have more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn net worldwide turnover, and non-EU companies must have EUR 1.5bn EU turnover. (Briefing p.3) - The Omnibus narrowed the liability and penalty provisions for CSDDD. (Briefing p.3)

title: SFDR
text: The Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) sets disclosure rules for asset managers, insurers, pension funds, and advisers in the EU. It mandates specific product labels based on ESG promotion or sustainable objectives, and SFDR 2.0 is planned to replace the current structure.

title: SFDR
text: - SFDR disclosure rules apply to asset managers, insurers, pension funds, and advisers. (Briefing pp.2-3) - Components of SFDR include entity-level principal adverse impact statements and product labels under Article 8 ("promotes" ESG) and Article 9 (sustainable objective). (Briefing pp.2-3) - SFDR 2.0 is expected to replace the current structure with three categories: Sustainable, Transition, and ESG Basics. (Briefing pp.2-3) - Each of the three SFDR 2.0 categories requires 70% of assets to meet the category's criteria. (Briefing pp.2-3) - SFDR 2.0 Council position was agreed upon in June 2026, and Parliament's committee position in September 2026; trilogues are expected to start in October. (Briefing pp.2-3) - SFDR is in scope for financial market participants and advisers marketing products in the EU, including non-EU managers. (Briefing pp.2-3) - Enforcement involves national financial regulators with ESMA coordinating, and greenwashing in fund names and marketing is an active enforcement priority. (Briefing pp.2-3)

title: VSME Standard
text: The Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard for non-listed SMEs (VSME) is a streamlined, accessible alternative to the ESRS designed to help small and medium-sized enterprises report on sustainability performance proportionate to their needs. It aids SMEs in responding to ESG demands from investors and corporate partners, thereby improving risk management and access to capital.

title: VSME Standard
text: - VSME offers a streamlined, accessible alternative to the ESRS. (Novata pp.2-3) - VSME helps SMEs report on sustainability performance in a way that is proportionate to their business needs. (Novata pp.2-3) - The VSME helps SMEs respond to ESG demands from investors and corporate partners in their value chain. (Novata pp.2-3) - The VSME helps SMEs improve risk management and access to capital. (Novata pp.2-3) - Companies have the flexibility to report based on what’s relevant and their reporting readiness through Basic and Comprehensive modules. (Novata pp.2-3) - VSME is aligned with the EU Omnibus I proposal and its “value chain cap” on sustainability data requests. (Novata pp.2-3) - VSME enables SMEs to demonstrate resilience, manage climate risks, and prepare for evolving regulations. (Novata pp.2-3)

title: CDP
text: CDP, formerly the Carbon Disclosure Project, is an international nonprofit organization that offers a leading environmental impact disclosure system. It allows various entities to assess greenhouse gas emissions and climate risks, helping to drive emissions reductions and strengthen climate resilience.

title: CDP
text: - CDP is an international nonprofit organization that provides the world’s leading environmental impact disclosure system. (Novata p.4) - It enables investors, companies, cities, states, and regions to assess their greenhouse gas emissions and climate risks, driving emissions reductions and strengthening climate resilience. (Novata p.4) - CDP collects and standardizes environmental data on a voluntary basis to better inform corporate and city progress towards climate change, forests, and water security goals through an independent scoring methodology. (Novata p.4) - Its focus is on environmental impact, particularly carbon emissions, with a global scope. (Comparison table, CDP row) - Reporting requirement is voluntary, but it is used by investors and governments. (Comparison table, CDP row) - It is aligned with SBTi, TCFD, and GRI. (Comparison table, CDP row) - It focuses on environmental disclosures, especially climate and water security. (Comparison table, CDP row)

title: GHG Protocol
text: The GHG Protocol is the accounting rulebook for emissions that every regime in the briefing relies on. It consists of the Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance (location- and market-based methods), and the Scope 3 Standard covering 15 value chain categories.

title: GHG Protocol
text: - Components include the Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance (location- and market-based methods), and the Scope 3 Standard (15 value chain categories). (Briefing pp.1-2) - A revision under consultation would require hourly and regional matching of renewable energy certificates for market-based Scope 2 claims. (Briefing pp.1-2) - A final standard is expected in 2027, with implementation likely from 2028. (Briefing pp.1-2) - It is an in-scope standard for Voluntary reporting. (Briefing pp.1-2) - It is referenced directly by California SB 253, ISSB, AASB S2, and ESRS. (Briefing pp.1-2) - Enforcement is not inherent; errors are penalized through the laws that reference it. (Briefing pp.1-2)

title: GRI Standards
text: GRI Standards are the most widely used impact-focused framework for sustainability reporting, designed for all stakeholders rather than just investors. They are built on the principle of impact materiality, requiring organizations to report on how their activities affect the economy, environment, and society.

title: GRI Standards
text: - GRI Standards are known as the most widely used standards for sustainability reporting, with over 70% of leading companies globally adopting it as a primary framework for disclosing ESG impact. (Novata p.3) - The GRI Standards are built on the principle of impact materiality, requiring organizations to report on how their activities affect the economy, environment, and society. (Novata p.3) - Components of the GRI Standards include Universal Standards (GRI 1 to 3), 30+ topic standards, and sector standards. (Briefing p.1) - New GRI 102 (Climate Change) and GRI 103 (Energy) apply to reports published from 1 January 2027, which add transition plan, just transition, and carbon credit disclosures. (Briefing p.1) - The GRI Standards are voluntary for any organization of any size or sector. (Briefing p.1) - Claiming "in accordance with GRI" requires a content index and notification to GRI; ESRS is designed to be interoperable with it. (Briefing p.1) - The GRI framework focuses on the wider impact of sustainability on stakeholders, beyond financial materiality. (Comparison table, GRI row)

title: ISSB Standards
text: The ISSB Standards (IFRS S1 and S2) are investor-focused global baseline standards from the IFRS Foundation designed to help investors and capital markets assess and disclose sustainability-related risks and opportunities. They cover general sustainability-related financial information (S1) and climate-related disclosures (S2).

title: ISSB Standards
text: - S1 covers general sustainability-related financial information. (Briefing p.1) - S2 covers climate-related disclosures. (Briefing p.1) - Both standards use the four TCFD pillars: governance, strategy, risk management, metrics and targets. (Briefing p.1) - Both standards require Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions and climate scenario analysis. (Briefing p.1) - Both standards apply a financial materiality lens. (Briefing p.1) - As of April 2026, 28 jurisdictions had adopted the standards on a voluntary or mandatory basis, and 12 more were planned to adopt them. (Briefing p.1) - Australia, Japan, the UK and Brazil have issued ISSB-based standards. (Briefing p.1) - Enforcement of the standards is done by the regulators that adopt them, not by the ISSB itself. (Briefing p.1)

title: Private Markets ESG Frameworks
text: Invest Europe and EDCI are frameworks designed for private equity and venture capital to address the fragmented approach to sustainability data collection and reporting. They aim to drive convergence around sustainability metrics to enable comparable reporting.

path: vault/wiki/Frameworks and Standards/Private Markets ESG Frameworks.md
title: Private Markets ESG Frameworks
text: - The ESG Data Convergence Initiative (EDCI) is a global private markets initiative focused on streamlining the industry’s approach to collecting and reporting sustainability data. (Novata pp.4-5) - The core metric categories reviewed annually by the EDCI currently include greenhouse gas emissions, diversity, and employee engagement. (Novata pp.4-5) - The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a set of 17 interconnected global goals designed to address the world’s most pressing social, environmental, and economic challenges by 2030. (Novata pp.4-5) - Invest Europe is a voluntary, principles-based ESG framework developed for European firms in the private equity, venture capital, and infrastructure sectors, and their investors. (Novata p.4) - Invest Europe provides guidance on integrating ESG considerations into the entire investment lifecycle, from evaluation to exit. (Novata p.4) - Invest Europe manages an ESG reporting template for reporting at the portfolio company, GP, and fund levels. (Novata p.4)

title: SASB Standards
text: SASB standards are industry-specific, voluntary disclosure standards focused on financially material sustainability issues relevant to investors. They are developed by the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board and aim to identify the most relevant ESG topics for each industry.

title: SASB Standards
text: - SASB focuses on industry-specific ESG performance. (Comparison table, SASB row) - SASB developed industry-specific disclosure guidance on sustainability-related risks and opportunities covering 77 industries. (Novata p.2) - The standards are designed to identify the most relevant environmental, social, and governance issues that may impact the financial performance and overall enterprise value of an organization. (Novata p.2) - SASB has an open standard-setting approach, allowing flexibility to determine what ESG topics are financially material to a business. (Novata p.2) - SASB focuses on financially material sustainability issues relevant to investors. (Comparison table, SASB row) - SASB standards set specific and detailed technical requirements on how sustainability data should be measured, reported, and verified. (Novata pp.1-2) - SASB is aligned with TCFD and GRI. (Comparison table, SASB row)

title: SBTi
text: The Science-Based Targets initiative (SBTi) is a framework focused on setting science-based corporate emissions reduction targets. It requires companies to commit to setting targets aligned with scientific goals, such as limiting global warming to 1.5°C.

title: SBTi
text: - Focus: Climate goals, GHG emissions reductions. (Comparison table, SBTi row) - Scope: Global. (Comparison table, SBTi row) - Reporting Requirement: Voluntary; companies commit to setting science-based emissions reduction targets. (Comparison table, SBTi row) - Key Features: Focuses on aligning corporate emissions reduction targets with scientific goals (e.g., limiting global warming to 1.5°C). (Comparison table, SBTi row) - Key Takeaways: Focuses on climate science. (Comparison table) - Key Takeaways: Focuses on industry-specific guidance and emissions targets, with emphasis on climate science. (Comparison table)

title: TCFD
text: The Task Force for Climate-Related Disclosures (TCFD) was established by the Financial Stability Board in 2015 to provide recommendations for climate-related financial information disclosure. It guides companies in being more transparent about climate-related risk exposures to investors, lenders, and insurance underwriters.

title: TCFD
text: - The TCFD is comprised of 11 recommendations structured around four pillars: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets. (Novata pp.3-4) - The TCFD was developed to guide disclosure recommendations for climate-related financial information. (Novata pp.3-4) - TCFD is focused on climate-related financial risk. (Comparison table, TCFD row) - TCFD emphasizes the financial impact of climate risks and includes scenario analysis. (Comparison table, TCFD row) - TCFD is a voluntary reporting requirement but is increasingly adopted in mandatory disclosure regimes. (Comparison table, TCFD row) - TCFD-aligned disclosures are now mandatory in many jurisdictions globally, including the UK, Japan, and New Zealand. (Novata pp.3-4) - The TCFD disbanded in October 2023, but the IFRS foundation incorporated the full TCFD recommendations in its publication of IFRS S1 and S2 standards. (Novata pp.3-4)

title: UN Sustainable Development Goals
text: The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a set of 17 interconnected global goals established to address the world’s most pressing social, environmental, and economic challenges by 2030. They serve as a high-level framework for aligning business strategy and capital allocation with broader societal outcomes.

path: vault/wiki/Frameworks and Standards/UN Sustainable Development Goals.md
title: UN Sustainable Development Goals
text: - The SDGs are a set of 17 interconnected global goals. (Novata pp.4-5) - The SDGs are designed to address the world’s most pressing social, environmental, and economic challenges by 2030. (Novata pp.4-5) - The SDGs span areas such as climate action, clean energy, gender equality, and responsible consumption. (Novata pp.4-5) - For companies and investors, the SDGs serve as a high-level framework for aligning business strategy and capital allocation with broader societal outcomes. (Novata pp.4-5)

title: Australia AASB S2
text: AASB S2 mandates climate reporting in Australia based on IFRS S2, requiring specific components like governance, strategy, risk management, and emissions reporting. This is mandatory under Chapter 2M of the Corporations Act 2001 and applies to entities meeting certain size tests, with phased implementation for different groups.

title: Australia AASB S2
text: - Mandatory climate reporting is under Chapter 2M of the Corporations Act 2001, based on IFRS S2. (Briefing p.4) - The sustainability report must cover governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics. (Briefing p.4) - Scope 1 and 2 emissions are reported from year one, and Scope 3 emissions from year two. (Briefing p.4) - Scenario analysis must be conducted at 1.5°C and at 2.5°C or higher. (Briefing p.4) - Assurance phasing moves from limited to reasonable. (Briefing p.4) - In scope entities are those that lodge annual reports and meet two of three size tests, phased by group. (Briefing p.4) - Group 1 began reporting years starting 1 January 2025 (revenue A$500m, assets A$1bn, 500 employees). (Briefing p.4) - Group 2 began reporting years starting 1 July 2026 (A$200m, A$500m, 250 employees). (Briefing p.4) - Group 3 follows from 1 July 2027 (A$50m, A$25m, 100 employees). (Briefing p.4) - Large emitters under the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Act and large asset owners are also included. (Briefing p.4) - Enforcement is handled by ASIC under the same civil penalty and director liability provisions as financial reports. (Briefing p.4) - A three-year "modified liability" period limits claims over Scope 3, scenario analysis, and transition plans to ASIC-only actions. (Briefing p.4)

title: India BRSR
text: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) is India's mandatory ESG report for the top 1,000 listed companies, set by SEBI. It requires reporting on nine principles, with a subset called BRSR Core requiring independent assessment or assurance.

title: India BRSR
text: - The Full BRSR covers the nine principles of India's National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct, spanning from environment to employee welfare to consumer fairness. (Briefing pp.4-5) - BRSR Core is a subset of nine attributes that must be independently assessed or assured. (Briefing pp.4-5) - BRSR Core assessment or assurance extends to all 1,000 listed companies from FY 2026-27. (Briefing pp.4-5) - The Full BRSR is filed by the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalization. (Briefing pp.4-5) - Value chain disclosures for the top 250 companies are voluntary from FY 2025-26 after SEBI's March 2025 deferral. (Briefing pp.4-5) - Listing obligation under SEBI's LODR Regulation 34(2)(f) requires filing the BRSR with the annual report. (Briefing pp.4-5) - SEBI and stock exchanges can impose fines and other actions for non-compliance or misstatement. (Briefing pp.4-5)

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: This note compares various ESG frameworks, highlighting their focus areas, scope, and reporting requirements. It is important because these frameworks guide corporate sustainability reporting and disclosure practices.

title: ESG Frameworks Comparison
text: - SASB focuses on industry-specific ESG performance and is voluntary but often integrated into financial disclosures. (Comparison table, SASB row) - SBTi focuses on climate goals and GHG emissions reductions, requiring companies to commit to science-based emissions reduction targets. (Comparison table, SBTi row) - CSRD requires comprehensive sustainability reporting for large EU companies, with a phased approach starting in 2024, and integrates double materiality. (Comparison table, CSRD row) - TCFD focuses on climate-related financial risk and emphasizes financial impact of climate risks through scenario analysis. (Comparison table, TCFD row) - GRI focuses on broad sustainability impacts on stakeholders beyond financial materiality and has sector-specific standards available. (Comparison table, GRI row) - CDP focuses on environmental impact, particularly carbon emissions, and is used by investors and governments. (Comparison table, CDP row) - ISSB aims to create globally consistent, comparable sustainability standards and integrates financial materiality. (Comparison table, ISSB row) - SASB focuses on industry-specific guidance, while SBTi focuses on emissions targets, with SASB emphasizing financial materiality and SBTi emphasizing climate science. (Comparison table)

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: This briefing outlines various global sustainability reporting frameworks, noting that while many are voluntary, they form the basis for mandatory regimes. These frameworks cover investor-focused standards (ISSB), stakeholder-focused standards (GRI), emissions accounting (GHG Protocol), and jurisdiction-specific regulations (CSRD, EU Taxonomy, California laws).

title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
text: - ISSB Standards (IFRS S1 and S2) cover general sustainability-related financial information (S1) and climate information (S2), using the four TCFD pillars, requiring Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, and applying a financial materiality lens. (Briefing p.1) - As of April 2026, 28 jurisdictions had adopted ISSB Standards voluntarily or mandatorily, with 12 more planned to adopt. (Briefing p.1) - GRI Standards are the most widely used impact-focused framework, built on impact materiality and covering Universal Standards (GRI 1 to 3) and 30+ topic standards. (Briefing p.1) - New GRI 102 (Climate Change) and GRI 103 (Energy) apply to reports published from 1 January 2027, adding transition plan, just transition, and carbon credit disclosures. (Briefing p.1) - The GHG Protocol is the accounting rulebook for emissions, including the Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance, and Scope 3 Standard (15 value chain categories). (Briefing pp.1-2) - The EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and ESRS are mandatory reporting laws for EU companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450m net turnover. (Briefing p.2) - The EU Taxonomy Regulation classifies economic activities as environmentally sustainable based on six environmental objectives, requiring companies to report the share of turnover, CapEx, and OpEx that is eligible and aligned. (Briefing p.2) - California SB 253 requires annual Scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting from 2026 and Scope 3 from 2027, measured under the GHG Protocol, with third-party assurance phasing from limited to reasonable. (Briefing pp.3-4) - The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) requires companies with more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn net worldwide turnover to identify, prevent, and remediate adverse human rights and environmental impacts by 26 July 2029. (Briefing p.3)

title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: ESG standards set specific technical requirements for measuring, reporting, and verifying sustainability data to ensure consistency and comparability. ESG frameworks, conversely, provide a broad, contextual approach defining themes and objectives for reporting, while standards prescribe exact metrics and methodologies.

path: vault/wiki/Sources/Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide.md
title: Novata ESG Standards and Frameworks Guide
text: - ESG standards set specific and detailed technical requirements on how sustainability data should be measured, reported, and verified, creating consistency for comparison. (Novata pp.1-2) - ESG frameworks provide a broad, contextual approach to ESG reporting by defining themes, objectives, and scope, guiding companies on topics, data collection, and presentation. (Novata p.3) - ESG standards are prescriptive, defining exact metrics and methodologies, which is valuable for investors needing to compare performance across a portfolio or industry benchmark. (Novata p.5) - ESG frameworks are broad and provide a contextual "frame" on how to disclose material topics, such as the TCFD, which leaves specific data points to the reporting company. (Novata p.5) - The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards are known as the most widely used standards for sustainability reporting, with over 70% of leading companies globally adopting it as a primary framework. (Novata p.3) - The Task Force on Climate-Related Disclosures (TCFD) was established by the Financial Stability Board in 2015 and is comprised of 11 recommendations structured around four pillars: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets. (Novata pp.3-4) - The International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) Sustainability Disclosure Standards, including IFRS S1 and IFRS S2, were published in 2023 and are seeing rapid regulatory uptake, with over 36 jurisdictions committed to aligning with them. (Novata p.2) - The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are a set of 17 interconnected global goals designed to address the world’s most pressing social, environmental, and economic challenges by 2030. (Novata pp.4-5)

title: California SB 253 and SB 261
text: California has enacted two companion laws, SB 253 and SB 261, administered by CARB, which mandate corporate climate data and financial risk reporting. These laws require annual Scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting starting in 2026 and biennial public reports on climate-related financial risk.

title: California SB 253 and SB 261
text: - SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) requires annual Scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting starting from 2026 and Scope 3 reporting from 2027, measured under the GHG Protocol. (Briefing pp.3-4) - Third-party assurance for SB 253 reporting is phasing from limited to reasonable. (Briefing pp.3-4) - SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act) requires a biennial public report on climate-related financial risk and mitigation, which may follow TCFD or ISSB. (Briefing pp.3-4) - SB 253 applies to US-organized entities doing business in California with total annual revenue above $1bn. (Briefing pp.3-4) - SB 261 applies to public or private entities with total annual revenue above $500m. (Briefing pp.3-4) - CARB moved the first SB 253 deadline from 10 August to 10 November 2026 and will not require assurance on that first report. (Briefing pp.3-4) - CARB administrative penalties under SB 253 are up to $500,000 per reporting year, and under SB 261 are up to $50,000. (Briefing pp.3-4) - Scope 3 misstatements are protected by a safe harbor if made in good faith, and penalties for Scope 3 are limited to non-filing until 2030. (Briefing pp.3-4)

title: SEC Climate Rule
text: The SEC's 2024 climate disclosure rule is currently stayed, meaning it has not taken effect. This rule was stayed in 2024, and the SEC stopped defending it in March 2025, with a proposal to rescind it on 29 May 2026. Until a final rescission, the 2010 interpretive guidance on material climate risk remains applicable. (Briefing p.3)

title: SEC Climate Rule
text: - There is no federal mandate; California is the binding regime. (Briefing p.3) - The SEC's 2024 climate rule never took effect. (Briefing p.3) - The rule was stayed in 2024. (Briefing p.3) - The SEC stopped defending the rule in March 2025. (Briefing p.3) - The SEC proposed rescinding the rule on 29 May 2026. (Briefing p.3) - Until a final rescission, the rule stays stayed. (Briefing p.3) - The SEC's 2010 interpretive guidance on material climate risk still applies. (Briefing p.3)
